The daily work of fast food and counter workers revolves around the shift cycle: check scheduling and shift change information and set up uniform, work counter and materials before the shift; use cash register and ordering equipment to record customer orders, calculate amounts and collect payment and give change, and issue receipts or send tickets to the back of house where necessary; take food from the serving counter or holding station according to the order, plate or package it and hand it to the customer; brew coffee and tea, make cold drinks and ice cream drinks, and heat or simply cook foods such as sandwiches, salads, soups and pizza while observing hygiene and safe operation; restock counter food and consumables and report shortages or special orders; clean the dining area, service counter, tableware and equipment and keep the work area hygienic; handle and store food according to hygiene requirements and monitor food temperature; and communicate with customers about orders, comments and complaints and hand over order and shift issues with colleagues and the shift manager.

paragraphs:
Work context｜Fast food and counter workers work on site in fast food restaurants, canteens, coffee and beverage shops, and takeaway and group catering settings, forming a shift cycle around ordering and payment, meal preparation and serving, material replenishment, cleaning and hygiene, and customer communication.
Work locations｜Fast food and fast casual outlets, school and corporate canteens, hospital and elder care catering, coffee and beverage shops, convenience stores and takeaway stalls.
Working conditions｜Mainly standing and walking physical work ("standing continually or almost continually" 54%, "walking continually or almost continually" 38%, "making repetitive motions continually or almost continually" 64% in O*NET work context); schedules are mainly regular shifts (88%), 63% of respondents work less than 40 hours per week and 17% more than 40 hours; shifts often include early, late, weekend and holiday work, and part-time work is common.

Main objects｜Food and beverages, tableware and packaging, ordering and cash register equipment, refrigeration and heating equipment, materials and consumables, and order and sales records.
Collaboration｜Working with colleagues, the shift manager or store manager, kitchen and back-of-house staff, delivery riders and customers.
Tools and materials｜Point-of-sale (POS) and ordering systems, beverage and ice cream machines, microwave and heating equipment, cleaning and disinfecting supplies, and menus and nutrition information sheets.

Institutional basis｜Food hygiene and safe operation requirements (including temperature and shelf life management), personal hygiene and hand cleaning requirements, fire safety and equipment operation requirements, employment and wage and hour rules (including tip and overtime rules), and local requirements for food business operations and public place hygiene.
Record requirements｜Order and cashier records, temperature and shelf life check records, cleaning and disinfection records, and inventory and requisition records must be documented according to employer rules.

Safety and jurisdictional boundaries｜Food hygiene and allergen notices, equipment and fire safety, and employment and settlement matters must be handled according to employer rules, competent authority requirements and local laws and regulations; matters involving allergens, food safety incidents or employment disputes must be confirmed by the shift manager, competent authorities or professionals, and this page does not provide food safety or legal advice.

entries.answer: Take orders, serve food and beverages and collect payment in fast food and counter service settings, and may take part in preparing simple food and drinks: record orders and close out bills using cash register and ordering equipment and verify the cash; take food from the serving counter or holding station according to the order, plate or package it and hand it to the customer; brew coffee and tea, make cold drinks and ice cream drinks, and heat or simply cook foods such as sandwiches, salads, soups and pizza; restock the counter and materials and report shortages; clean the dining area, service counter, tableware and equipment and keep the work area hygienic; handle and store food according to hygiene requirements and monitor food temperature; and communicate with customers about orders, comments and complaints.
entries.question: What do fast food and counter workers mainly do?

entries.answer: The objects of responsibility differ: this occupation takes orders at the counter, provides food and beverages and collects payment, and may take part in simple food preparation and cleaning; fast food cooks focus on quick cooking in the back of house; waiters and waitresses focus on taking orders, serving food and providing tableside service in dine-in settings; counter and rental clerks handle rental, return and registration business; cashiers focus on merchandise checkout and payment; dishwashers focus on back-of-house washing and kitchen cleaning; first-line supervisors of food preparation and serving workers are responsible for scheduling, task assignment and service quality supervision; and food service managers are responsible for store operations, costs and personnel management.
entries.question: How does it differ from fast food cooks and waiters and waitresses?

entries.answer: O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone 1–2 (little to some preparation), SVP below 6.0; in the education survey about 56% indicated below a high school diploma, 24% indicated a high school diploma or equivalent and 17% indicated some college education but no degree. BLS notes that the typical entry-level education for this occupation requires no formal credential and no related work experience, with short-term on-the-job training provided. Posts involving food handling must comply with local health and hygiene requirements for food handlers and receive food hygiene and equipment operation training. In mainland China, store training plus on-the-job practice is commonly required, and the specifics are subject to recruitment announcements and local provisions.
entries.question: What education and qualifications are needed?

entries.answer: A more accurate judgment is that some tasks will be assisted by tools and that the occupation as a whole will mainly see augmentation and structural adjustment. A 2023 ILO study shows that task exposure varies widely across occupations and that technical feasibility does not mean stores have already adopted it; meanwhile on-site service, food temperature and hygiene judgments, and handling equipment and customer emergencies require on-site work and responsibility, so the conclusion is that the way of working will change rather than that the occupation as a whole will be replaced.
entries.question: Will this occupation be replaced by AI?

entries.answer: No. The median is the midpoint of the wage distribution of practitioners within the same statistical period, not a starting salary. Part-time work is common in this occupation and some posts include tips or service charges; personal income must be judged together with the pay method (hourly or monthly, whether tips or service charges are included) and actual hours (O*NET work context shows 63% of respondents work less than 40 hours per week and 17% more than 40 hours).
entries.question: Is the United States median an entry-level wage?

entries.answer: Yes. BLS notes that the typical entry-level education for this occupation requires no formal credential and no related work experience, with short-term on-the-job training provided, and most posts are taken up through mentoring. However, posts involving food handling usually require compliance with local health and hygiene requirements for food handlers and specialized training; whether cashiering and reconciliation are required, whether simple back-of-house cooking is involved, and shift and part-time arrangements all vary by store. Whether it is feasible depends on the target employer and local provisions, and this page does not replace the original regulations.
